jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 8: whether theology is subalternated to metaphysics.

jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e113.summary: First argument that theology is subalternated to metaphysics: metaphysics gives the propter quid of what theology holds as quia—theology says God is one, metaphysics says why, namely because he is the first and wholly perfect being, which can only be one.
claims: Metaphysics gives the reason why God is one, which theology only asserts (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e137.summary: Second argument: theology presupposes and uses as principles what metaphysics proves—that God is one (Metaphysics II) and the principle of non-contradiction—so it is subalternated to metaphysics.
claims: Theology uses principles proved in metaphysics, including divine unity and non-contradiction (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e158.summary: Contrary argument that theology subalternates human sciences, first the practical ones: the science of the ultimate end subalternates those of intermediate ends, and theology concerns the ultimate end.
claims: Theology, as science of the ultimate end, subalternates practical sciences of intermediate ends (counter-argument)

jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e176.summary: Second contrary argument, regarding speculative sciences: theology gives the propter quid of their principles, e.g. natural science says a thing has a certain power, and theology says why—because God willed to give it.
claims: Theology gives the cause of natural powers in God's will (counter-argument)

jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e192.summary: Response divided into whether theology subalternates other sciences and whether it is subalternated to them. First: it does not subalternate them, because sciences that have more evident knowledge of their principles than theology could provide are not subalternated to it. Proper subalternation means the lower depends on the higher for perfect knowledge of its principles, and evidence pertains more to perfection of knowledge than adhesion (which can be to falsehood); human sciences have clear evidence of their principles via sense, memory, and experience, whereas theology's knowledge of them would be only enigmatic, by authority.
claims: Theology does not subalternate humanly devised sciences
Evidence pertains more to the perfection of knowledge than firmness of adhesion
Human sciences know their principles evidently through sense, memory, and experience; theology knows only enigmatically by authority

jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e240.summary: Second: theology is not subalternated to any human science, because it depends more on the science of God and the blessed than on any human science and is not properly subalternated even to that (Q7); and no mode of subalternation holds—no other science's subject is the end of theology's subject (rather the reverse), and no human science gives the cause of what theology holds as quia.
claims: Theology is not subalternated to any humanly devised science
No mode of proper subalternation holds between theology and human sciences

jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e275.summary: Reply to the first argument: that God is one has no cause; being the first, simplest, wholly perfect being infallibly entails his unity and can be our means of knowing it, but is not its cause, so metaphysics gives no propter quid.
claims: God's unity has no cause
A middle of knowing need not be a cause of the thing known

jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e297.summary: Reply to the second: presupposing and using what another science proves does not suffice for subalternation, else all sciences would be subalternated to logic. Assuming as principles what another science proves a priori would contribute to subalternation, but theology takes nothing such from metaphysics: it holds God's unity by divine authority, on which it relies more than on any human reason, and metaphysics proves it only a posteriori. The principle of non-contradiction is self-evident to anyone who understands the terms; metaphysics only defends it against verbal denial.
claims: Using another science's results does not by itself make a science subalternate
Theology holds God's unity by divine authority, not from metaphysics
Metaphysics proves God's unity only a posteriori
The principle of non-contradiction is self-evident, not derived from metaphysics

jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e346.summary: Reply to the first contrary argument: the science of the ultimate end subalternates others only if they consider their subjects as ordered to it (as bridle-making considers the bridle for riding) and the higher evidently gives the propter quid of their principles; neither holds between theology and practical sciences.
claims: Human practical sciences do not consider their subjects as ordered to theology's end
Theology does not evidently give the propter quid of their principles

jsnvu6-d1e166-d1e375.summary: Reply to the last argument, that God's will as cause of things gives the propter quid of other sciences' principles, which fails for three reasons: a subalternate science must take its propter quid from the subalternating one, but that God causes by will is knowable by natural reason; this propter quid is only a remote cause; and it does not make the quia evident—rather we know God's will from observing that an herb has a given power, not conversely.
claims: That God causes things by his will is knowable by natural reason
A remote cause does not suffice for proper subalternation
We come to know God's will regarding natural powers from the powers themselves, not the reverse

jsnvu6-d1e166.summary: Question 8 completes the comparison of theology with other sciences by asking whether it is subalternated to metaphysics, and more broadly whether it subalternates or is subalternated to humanly devised sciences. Durandus answers no on both counts. Theology does not subalternate human sciences, because they possess clearer evidence of their principles through sense, memory, and experience than theology's enigmatic, authority-based knowledge could provide, and evidence counts more than adhesion for the perfection of knowledge. Nor is theology subalternated to them: it depends more on the science of the blessed and is not properly subalternated even to that, and no mode of subalternation (end–means or effect–cause) holds. Metaphysics gives no propter quid of God's unity, which has no cause; theology holds that truth by divine authority, while metaphysics proves it only a posteriori; and the first principle is self-evident rather than taken from metaphysics. Conversely, theology's appeal to God's will as the cause of natural powers is only a remote cause, knowable by natural reason, and known from the effects rather than making them evident.
claims: Theology does not subalternate humanly devised sciences
Theology is not subalternated to metaphysics or any human science
God's unity has no cause, so metaphysics gives no propter quid of it
Theology holds God's unity by divine authority rather than receiving it from metaphysics
God's will as cause of things is only a remote cause and does not ground subalternation
